q: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
p: ENTRYPOINT defines the executable; CMD supplies default arguments or a default command. Arguments to docker run replace CMD but append to ENTRYPOINT.
tip: Use exec form so signals reach the process.
a: ENTRYPOINT sets the program the container runs, and CMD provides default arguments to it, or a default command if no entrypoint exists. When I run the image with extra arguments, they replace CMD but are appended to ENTRYPOINT, so a well-built image behaves like a command-line tool: the entrypoint is the binary and CMD holds sensible defaults. Both should use the exec form, a JSON array, not the shell form. The shell form wraps the process in a shell, which becomes process one and may not forward SIGTERM, so the application will not shut down gracefully and Kubernetes waits until the kill timeout. If I need environment preparation, I write an entrypoint script that ends with exec on the real process, so it replaces the shell. To override the entrypoint for debugging, I use the entrypoint flag on docker run. Knowing this helps with containers that ignore stop signals.
f: Why use exec form?
How do you override the entrypoint for debugging?

q: What is the difference between COPY and ADD, and which should you use?
p: COPY copies local files; ADD also extracts local archives and fetches URLs. Prefer COPY for predictability.
tip: Use COPY unless you need tar extraction.
a: Both instructions add files to the image, but ADD has extra features: it can fetch a remote URL and automatically extract a local tar archive. Those features make behaviour less obvious, and a remote download inside ADD adds no checksum verification and cannot be cached or cleaned up in the same layer. So best practice is to use COPY for plain file copying, since what it does is explicit, and to use a RUN step with curl, a checksum verification and cleanup for downloads. ADD is acceptable when I deliberately want to unpack a local archive, such as a root filesystem, into the image. I also set ownership with the chown flag to avoid running everything as root, and I order COPY instructions from least to most frequently changing, so that the layer cache stays effective. Clear instructions make images reproducible and easier to review.
f: Why avoid ADD for URLs?
How does COPY ordering affect caching?

q: How do ARG and ENV differ in a Dockerfile, and what are the secret-leak risks?
p: ARG exists only at build time; ENV persists into the image and runtime. Both are visible in image history, so never pass secrets through them.
tip: Use BuildKit secret mounts for secrets.
a: ARG defines a variable that is available only while building, and can be set with the build-arg flag. ENV sets an environment variable that is stored in the image configuration and visible to the running container. The security problem is that both are recorded: anyone with the image can run history or inspect and read ARG values used in commands and ENV values. So passing a token as a build argument to download a private package leaks it into the image. The correct approach is BuildKit secret mounts, which expose a secret file to a single RUN step without writing it into any layer, or SSH agent forwarding for private repositories. Runtime secrets should be injected by the orchestrator at start, not baked in. I also remember that ARG values declared before FROM are not available after it unless redeclared, and that changing an ARG busts the cache from the point of use.
f: Why is ARG not safe for secrets?
What is a BuildKit secret mount?

q: What happens when you run docker stop, and why do containers sometimes take ten seconds to stop?
p: Docker sends SIGTERM, waits the grace period, then sends SIGKILL. Delays mean the process ignores or never receives SIGTERM.
a: Docker stop sends SIGTERM, or the image's configured stop signal, to the main process of the container, waits for the timeout, which is ten seconds by default, and then sends SIGKILL. If a container always takes the full ten seconds, the application is not handling SIGTERM. Common reasons are the shell form of CMD, where the shell is PID one and does not forward the signal, an entrypoint script that does not use exec, or an application that has no signal handler; as PID one, Linux does not apply default signal actions, so without a handler the signal is ignored. Fixes include using the exec form, adding exec to scripts, implementing graceful shutdown in the application, or using a tiny init such as tini through the init flag, which forwards signals and reaps zombies. In Kubernetes the same applies with the termination grace period, and a preStop hook helps drain connections.
f: Why is PID 1 special?
What does the init flag do?

q: How do you clean up disk space used by Docker safely on a build host?
p: Inspect with docker system df, prune dangling images, stopped containers, unused networks and build cache with age filters.
a: I start by looking at usage with docker system df, which breaks down images, containers, local volumes and build cache. Then I prune in order of safety. Stopped containers and dangling images can be removed freely. For unused images, I use the all option with an until filter, so recent images that are probably still in use remain. Build cache can grow very large on CI hosts, so I cap it with builder prune and a keep-storage limit. Volume pruning is the dangerous one because it can delete data for stopped containers' named volumes, so I avoid it automatically and only do it after checking what is unused. On shared CI runners, I schedule the cleanup and also use ephemeral runners so the problem disappears. I also check the container log size, because unrotated JSON logs are a common hidden cause of full disks, and set max-size and max-file options.
f: Why is volume prune risky?
What else fills the disk?

q: What is Docker's restart policy and how does it differ from Kubernetes restarts?
p: Policies like no, on-failure, always and unless-stopped control daemon-level restarts; Kubernetes uses pod restartPolicy and controllers.
tip: Use on-failure with a cap for crash loops.
a: Docker restart policies tell the daemon what to do when a container exits. No means never restart; on-failure restarts only on non-zero exit and can have a maximum retry count; always restarts regardless and also on daemon start; unless-stopped is like always but respects a manual stop across daemon restarts. This gives basic self-healing on a single host. It lacks health awareness beyond the process exit, scheduling to other nodes and rescheduling when the host fails. Kubernetes handles this in layers: the pod restartPolicy governs restarts by the kubelet with exponential backoff, which produces CrashLoopBackOff, while controllers like Deployments replace pods and the scheduler places them on healthy nodes. Probes add health awareness. For a single-node setup, unless-stopped plus a health check is reasonable; for anything important, I use an orchestrator. I verify the result in a staging cluster before relying on it in production. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: What is the difference between always and unless-stopped?
What does CrashLoopBackOff mean?

q: How do you copy files in and out of containers and when is it appropriate?
p: docker cp works for debugging; production data should use volumes or object storage, not manual copies.
a: Docker cp copies files between a container and the host, whether the container is running or stopped, and kubectl cp does the same for pods. They are useful for debugging, such as extracting a heap dump, a log file or a generated report. They are not a deployment mechanism, because anything changed inside a container's writable layer disappears when it is replaced. If a workflow regularly needs files in or out, the design should change: mount a volume or bind mount for shared data, push artifacts to object storage, or ship logs to a log system. Kubectl cp depends on tar being present in the container, which distroless images lack, so I use ephemeral debug containers or exec with other means in those cases. I also watch for sensitive data in dumps and clean up copied files afterwards.
f: Why doesn't kubectl cp work in distroless images?
What is a better approach for regular file exchange?

q: How do you choose a base image: Alpine, Debian slim, distroless or scratch?
p: Balance size, compatibility, debuggability and attack surface. Alpine uses musl, distroless has no shell, scratch is empty for static binaries.
tip: Smaller is not always better if it breaks libc compatibility.
a: The base image determines size, security surface and compatibility. Debian slim variants are a safe default: moderately small, glibc-based and widely compatible. Alpine is very small and uses musl libc, which can cause subtle problems or slow builds for software with native extensions, such as some Python wheels, and DNS behaviour differences. Distroless images contain only the runtime and certificates, with no shell or package manager, reducing vulnerabilities and attacker tools, but making debugging harder, which I address with ephemeral debug containers. Scratch is completely empty and fits statically linked binaries, like Go programs. I also consider vendor-maintained minimal images, how quickly security patches arrive, and the ability to pin by digest. Whatever I choose, I rebuild regularly to pick up patches, run as a non-root user, and standardise on a small set of approved bases across the organisation.
f: What problems can musl cause?
How do you debug a distroless container?

q: How do you make image builds reproducible?
p: Pin base images by digest, pin package versions, use lock files, avoid latest and timestamps, and build in a controlled environment.
a: Reproducible means building the same inputs produces the same image. I pin the base image by digest rather than tag, since tags move. I pin operating system package versions where practical, or accept controlled drift with scheduled rebuilds, and I install language dependencies from lock files with hashes. I avoid commands that fetch whatever is current, such as curl of a latest script without a checksum. Build steps should not embed timestamps or random values, and I set SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH for tools that support normalising dates. The build runs in a clean, controlled environment with a pinned builder version, and I record provenance and an SBOM. Perfect bit-for-bit reproducibility is hard, but even reaching consistent dependency versions greatly improves debugging, security patching and audits, because I can state exactly what ran in production.
f: Why pin by digest?
What does SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH do?

q: How do you reduce image size without breaking the application?
p: Multi-stage builds, slim bases, combined RUN steps with cleanup, dockerignore, and removing build tools and caches.
cmds: RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
tip: Cleanup must be in the same layer.
a: Smaller images pull faster, start faster and have fewer vulnerabilities. The biggest win is a multi-stage build: compile and package in a builder stage with all the tools, then copy only the final artifacts into a slim runtime stage. Then I choose a small base, install packages with no-install-recommends, and remove package caches in the same RUN instruction, because deleting files in a later layer does not shrink earlier ones. A dockerignore file keeps the build context and image free of git history, tests and local files. I avoid installing debugging tools in production images, strip debug symbols when appropriate, and check what takes space with docker history or a tool like dive. I validate that nothing needed at runtime was removed by running tests against the final image, since overly aggressive trimming can break dynamic libraries or certificates.
f: Why must cleanup be in the same layer?
How do you inspect what makes an image large?

q: What is an image digest versus a tag, and why does it matter for deployments?
p: A tag is a movable label; a digest is the immutable content hash. Deploy by digest for exact, verifiable artifacts.
a: A tag such as 1.4 or latest is just a pointer in a registry and can be moved to a different image at any time, by accident or by an attacker. A digest is the SHA-256 hash of the image manifest; it identifies exactly one set of bytes. Deploying by digest ensures that every replica, in every cluster, runs the same image, and that rollbacks restore the exact earlier artifact. It also lets signature and scan results be tied to the specific image. In practice, CI tags images with the commit SHA for readability but records and deploys the digest, and manifests in Git reference it, often updated by automation. Kubernetes with a tag can behave differently across nodes if the tag changed and image pull policy forces a re-pull. Admission policies can also require digests or signatures.
f: Why is latest dangerous?
How do you find an image digest?

q: How do you run containers as non-root and why does it matter?
p: Create a user in the image, set USER, drop capabilities and, in Kubernetes, set runAsNonRoot and a read-only root filesystem.
a: By default, processes in a container run as root, and while namespaces limit what that means, a container escape or a mounted host path turns root inside into a much bigger problem. Running as an unprivileged user limits damage from application vulnerabilities, prevents writing to system files and satisfies security baselines. In the Dockerfile I create a dedicated user with a fixed numeric UID and switch with USER, and make sure the directories the application writes to are owned by it. In Kubernetes, I enforce this with runAsNonRoot, runAsUser, a read-only root filesystem with writable emptyDir mounts where necessary, dropping all capabilities, and disabling privilege escalation, and I use admission policies to reject non-compliant pods. Binding to ports below 1024 needs a capability or a higher port with a service mapping, which is a common stumbling block when migrating existing images.
f: Why a numeric UID?
How do you handle privileged ports?

q: What are Linux namespaces and cgroups, and how do containers use them?
p: Namespaces isolate what a process sees; cgroups limit what it can use. A container is a process with both applied.
a: A container is not a separate machine but a normal Linux process with restricted view and resources. Namespaces provide isolation of what the process can see: PID for its own process tree, network for interfaces and routing, mount for the filesystem view, UTS for hostname, IPC, user for ID mapping and cgroup. Control groups, or cgroups, limit and account for resource usage such as CPU, memory, I/O and number of processes; exceeding a memory limit triggers the OOM killer inside that group. The runtime combines these with a root filesystem from the image layers, restricted capabilities, seccomp filters and security modules like AppArmor or SELinux. Because all containers share the host kernel, a kernel vulnerability affects all, which is why stronger isolation like gVisor or microVMs exists. Understanding this explains behaviour such as seeing host CPU counts and limits applying only through cgroups.
f: What does the PID namespace do?
What happens when a cgroup memory limit is exceeded?

q: What is the difference between runc, containerd, CRI-O and Docker?
p: runc is the low-level OCI runtime; containerd and CRI-O are higher-level runtimes managing images and lifecycle; Docker adds a developer-friendly engine on top.
a: The stack has layers. At the bottom, runc is an OCI-compliant tool that actually creates the container using namespaces, cgroups and the root filesystem, then exits. Above it, containerd and CRI-O are daemons that pull images, manage snapshots and storage, handle networking hooks and supervise containers by calling runc. Kubernetes talks to them through the Container Runtime Interface, and since the removal of dockershim, clusters use containerd or CRI-O directly. Docker is a full developer experience: CLI, build system, image management and API, running on top of containerd. In a node, I use crictl to inspect CRI containers rather than docker commands. Alternative low-level runtimes like gVisor's runsc or Kata Containers plug in at the same level as runc for stronger isolation, selected in Kubernetes through RuntimeClass. I write the reasoning into the runbook so the on-call engineer understands it. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: What did the dockershim removal change?
What is a RuntimeClass?

q: How do you investigate a container killed by OOM, and how do you set memory limits properly?
p: Check exit code 137 and OOMKilled in status, review memory metrics, then size requests and limits from observed usage with headroom.
cmds: kubectl describe pod p | grep -A5 'Last State'
tip: Heap limits must sit below container limits.
a: An OOM-killed container shows exit code 137 and a reason OOMKilled in its last state. I check the memory usage trend in monitoring before the kill to distinguish a leak, a spike from load or a limit set too low. Kernel messages on the node confirm the cgroup that hit the limit. For runtimes with managed memory, like the JVM, I make sure the heap maximum is set relative to the container limit, leaving room for metaspace, thread stacks and native memory, otherwise the process grows beyond the cgroup limit even though the heap looks fine. I size requests from typical usage and limits from the observed peak plus headroom, and use memory limits equal to requests for critical pods to get predictable behaviour. If it is a leak, I use profilers and heap dumps to fix it instead of raising limits indefinitely.
f: What does exit code 137 mean?
Why can a JVM exceed the container limit?

q: How does CPU limiting work in containers and why can it cause latency?
p: CPU limits use CFS quota per period; hitting the quota throttles the process even when the node has idle CPU.
a: Kubernetes CPU requests translate to relative CPU shares used for scheduling and contention, while limits use the CFS bandwidth controller: the container gets a quota of CPU time per hundred-millisecond period. A multi-threaded application can burn its whole quota in a few milliseconds across several cores and then be paused until the next period, even though the node has idle CPU. This throttling shows up as latency spikes, particularly at the tail, and is easy to miss because average CPU utilisation looks low. I detect it using the throttled periods metrics from cAdvisor. Mitigations include raising or removing CPU limits while keeping requests accurate, which many teams do for latency-sensitive services, tuning thread pool sizes to the CPU count, and using the static CPU manager policy for guaranteed workloads. The trade-off of no limit is noisy neighbours, so monitoring matters.
f: How do you detect throttling?
Why do some teams remove CPU limits?

q: What is the container lifecycle from image pull to termination in Kubernetes?
p: Schedule, pull image, create sandbox and network, run init containers, start containers with probes, serve traffic, then preStop and SIGTERM on termination.
a: After the scheduler assigns a pod to a node, the kubelet asks the runtime to create the pod sandbox and set up networking via the CNI plugin. Volumes are mounted, images are pulled according to pull policy, and init containers run to completion in order. Then the main containers start. Startup, readiness and liveness probes determine when it is considered started, when it receives traffic from services, and when it is restarted. During normal operation the kubelet restarts failed containers according to the restart policy with backoff. On termination, the pod is marked as terminating and removed from service endpoints, the preStop hook runs, SIGTERM is sent, the grace period counts down, and finally SIGKILL if needed. Understanding the phases helps debug states like ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff, Init errors and slow shutdowns, since each points to a specific stage.
f: What happens to endpoints during termination?
What is the pod sandbox?

q: How does Docker's default bridge network provide NAT and DNS, and how do user-defined bridges differ?
p: The default bridge uses iptables NAT and no name resolution between containers; user-defined bridges add automatic DNS and better isolation.
a: On a single host, Docker creates a bridge device and connects each container with a virtual ethernet pair. Outbound traffic is masquerade NAT through iptables, and published ports use DNAT rules to forward host ports to container IPs. The default bridge does not provide name resolution between containers, so you would need legacy links or IP addresses. A user-defined bridge network provides an embedded DNS server, so containers reach each other by name or alias, and it offers better isolation because only containers on that network can talk to each other. Containers can join multiple networks. I use user-defined networks for compose stacks and local development. Multi-host communication needs overlay networks or an orchestrator's networking. When debugging, I check the bridge, veth interfaces, iptables rules and the container's resolv.conf. I verify the result in a staging cluster before relying on it in production. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: Why is DNS missing on the default bridge?
How are published ports implemented?

q: How do you debug DNS problems inside a container or pod?
p: Check resolv.conf, test lookups with nslookup or dig, review CoreDNS logs and ndots behaviour, and test search domains.
a: I start inside the container, examining resolv.conf for the nameserver, search domains and the ndots option. Then I test resolving a cluster service name, an external name and a fully qualified name with a trailing dot, using nslookup or dig, from a debug container if the image lacks tools. If cluster names fail but external names work, or the reverse, that points to different layers: CoreDNS, upstream resolvers or network policies blocking port 53. I review CoreDNS logs and metrics for errors, timeouts and SERVFAIL, and check that its pods are healthy and not overloaded. A classic cause of slowness is the default ndots of five, which makes unqualified external names try many search suffixes first, multiplying queries; using fully qualified names or lowering ndots helps. Intermittent five-second delays can indicate conntrack races with UDP, mitigated by node local DNS caching.
f: What does ndots do?
What is node-local DNS cache for?

q: What is the difference between ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and Ingress?
p: ClusterIP is internal; NodePort exposes on each node; LoadBalancer provisions a cloud LB; Ingress routes HTTP by host and path through a controller.
tip: One Ingress can front many services.
a: A ClusterIP service gives a stable virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster and is the default for internal communication. NodePort opens the same port on every node and forwards to the service, useful for testing and as a building block, but awkward for production. LoadBalancer asks the cloud provider to provision an external load balancer pointing at the service, which is simple but creates one balancer per service, costing money. Ingress is an HTTP layer resource: rules map hostnames and paths to services, implemented by a controller such as NGINX or a cloud load balancer, so one entry point serves many services with TLS termination. The newer Gateway API offers a more expressive, role-oriented model. I choose ClusterIP internally, Ingress or Gateway for web traffic, and LoadBalancer for non-HTTP protocols or when a dedicated address is required.
f: Why not a LoadBalancer per service?
What is the Gateway API?

q: How does kube-proxy implement Services, and what are iptables versus IPVS modes?
p: kube-proxy programs node rules that translate service virtual IPs to pod endpoints; iptables mode is rule-chain based, IPVS uses kernel load balancing with better scale.
tip: Services have no process listening on the VIP.
a: A service IP is virtual: no process listens on it. Kube-proxy on each node watches services and endpoints and programs the kernel to rewrite traffic destined for the service IP to one of the healthy pod IPs. In iptables mode it creates chains of rules with random probability to pick a backend; this works well but updates and lookups slow down with tens of thousands of services because rules are evaluated linearly. IPVS mode uses the kernel's load balancer with hash tables, giving constant-time lookups and more algorithms, such as least connections. Some CNIs, like Cilium, replace kube-proxy with eBPF programs for better performance and visibility. Connection tracking underlies these methods, so conntrack table exhaustion can cause dropped connections on busy nodes. Knowing this helps debug why a service does not route when endpoints are empty.
f: Why is IPVS better at scale?
How can conntrack cause problems?

q: How does service discovery work in Docker Compose and Kubernetes, and what are the pitfalls of caching DNS?
p: Both give services DNS names; clients that cache resolved IPs forever can miss changes after pods are replaced.
tip: Honour DNS TTL in your client.
a: In Compose, each service is reachable by its service name on the project's network through Docker's embedded DNS. In Kubernetes, services get names like service.namespace.svc.cluster.local, resolved by CoreDNS, and headless services return pod IPs directly. The pitfall is client-side caching. Some runtimes, like older JVM defaults, cache lookups indefinitely, and connection pools keep long-lived connections, so when pods are replaced or a database fails over, clients keep talking to a dead IP. I configure DNS TTL honouring in the runtime, set connection lifetimes and health checks in pools, and use retries with re-resolution. For stable service IPs the ClusterIP hides pod churn, but for headless services and external databases the client must handle changes. Testing failover deliberately reveals these issues before an incident does. I write the reasoning into the runbook so the on-call engineer understands it. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: What is a headless service?
How do connection pools hide failover problems?

q: What is the difference between PersistentVolume, PersistentVolumeClaim and StorageClass?
p: A PV is storage; a PVC is a request for it; a StorageClass defines how to dynamically provision PVs.
tip: Reclaim policy decides what happens on delete.
a: A PersistentVolume represents a piece of storage in the cluster, either created by an administrator or dynamically provisioned. A PersistentVolumeClaim is a request by a workload for storage with a size, access mode and optionally a class; the control plane binds it to a matching volume. A StorageClass describes a type of storage and its provisioner and parameters, such as disk type, replication or encryption, and enables dynamic provisioning: creating a claim automatically creates the underlying disk. Important settings include the volume binding mode, where wait-for-first-consumer delays provisioning until a pod is scheduled so the disk lands in the right zone, the reclaim policy, where delete removes the disk with the claim and retain keeps it, and allowVolumeExpansion. For StatefulSets, claim templates create one claim per replica. I back up important volumes with snapshots because deletion of a claim can destroy data.
f: Why use WaitForFirstConsumer?
What does the reclaim policy control?

q: What are the access modes ReadWriteOnce, ReadOnlyMany, ReadWriteMany and ReadWriteOncePod?
p: They define how many nodes or pods can mount a volume and with what permission; block disks are usually RWO, shared file systems support RWX.
tip: RWO limits to one node, not one pod.
a: ReadWriteOnce allows the volume to be mounted read-write by a single node; multiple pods on that node can still use it. ReadOnlyMany allows many nodes to mount it read-only, and ReadWriteMany allows many nodes to read and write, which requires a shared file system such as NFS, Filestore or EFS, because ordinary block disks cannot be attached to many nodes. ReadWriteOncePod restricts to a single pod in the whole cluster. These modes matter when scaling or rolling updates: with a Deployment using an RWO volume, a new pod scheduled to a different node cannot attach until the old one releases it, causing stuck rollouts, so I use the Recreate strategy or a StatefulSet. If an application needs shared storage across replicas, I consider whether object storage or a database would be a better architecture than a shared file system.
f: Why do RWO volumes block rolling updates?
When is object storage better than RWX?

q: How do you handle a full volume on a running stateful workload?
p: Identify what consumes space, free it safely or expand the PVC online if the class allows, and add alerts and retention.
a: First I confirm the usage with df inside the pod, then find the largest directories and whether growth is logs, temporary files, write-ahead logs or real data. For quick relief I remove safe items such as old logs or compacted data according to the application's guidance, not by randomly deleting database files. For a durable fix I expand the claim: if the storage class allows volume expansion, I patch the requested size, and the controller resizes the disk and then the file system, often online, though some drivers need a pod restart. Shrinking is generally impossible, so I size with headroom. Afterwards I add monitoring on free space percentage and on predicted time to full, set retention and rotation policies, and make sure backups exist before any risky action. For databases, an out-of-disk condition can cause corruption or readonly mode, so urgency is high.
f: Can volumes be shrunk?
What alerts prevent this?

q: How do volume snapshots and backups work for containerised stateful workloads?
p: CSI snapshots capture a point-in-time copy of a volume; application-consistent backups also need quiescing or native tools.
a: With CSI snapshot support, a VolumeSnapshot object triggers the storage backend to take a point-in-time copy of a volume, and I can create a new claim from that snapshot to restore or clone. These snapshots are crash-consistent, meaning like a power loss at that moment; databases usually recover from them but for guaranteed consistency I flush and lock tables, use the database's own backup tool, or pre-and-post hooks. Tools such as Velero back up Kubernetes resources together with volume snapshots or file-level copies to object storage, enabling cluster-level disaster recovery and migration. I store backups in a different failure domain, encrypt them, apply retention and, critically, test restores on a schedule, since an untested backup is only a hope. I also define recovery point and recovery time objectives, which decide how frequently to snapshot and how restore is rehearsed.
f: What is crash-consistent versus application-consistent?
What does Velero back up?

q: What are emptyDir and ephemeral volumes, and when should containers use them?
p: emptyDir is scratch space tied to the pod lifetime, optionally memory-backed; use it for caches and temporary files, not persistent data.
cmds:
volumes:
- name: tmp
  emptyDir:
    medium: Memory
    sizeLimit: 256Mi
tip: Set sizeLimit to avoid node pressure.
a: An emptyDir volume is created when a pod is assigned to a node and deleted when the pod is removed, so it survives container restarts but not pod replacement. It is shared by all containers in the pod, which makes it handy for scratch space, caches, sidecar file exchange, or providing writable directories when the root filesystem is read-only. The medium can be the node's disk or memory using tmpfs, which is fast but counts toward the container's memory limit. Without a size limit, a runaway process can fill the node's disk and trigger evictions, so I set sizeLimit and monitor ephemeral storage usage. Generic ephemeral volumes allow a per-pod claim from a storage class for larger scratch needs. Anything that must survive pod rescheduling belongs in a persistent volume or external storage.
f: What survives a container restart?
Why set sizeLimit?

q: How do maxSurge and maxUnavailable control a rolling update?
p: maxSurge sets how many extra pods can be created above desired; maxUnavailable sets how many may be unavailable; together they set rollout speed and capacity.
a: In a rolling update, the Deployment controller replaces old pods with new ones gradually. Max surge is how many pods above the desired replica count may exist temporarily; max unavailable is how many pods below desired may be unavailable during the update. Setting max unavailable to zero with a surge of one or a percentage means new pods must become ready before old ones are removed, preserving full capacity, at the cost of needing extra resources and a slower rollout. Allowing unavailability speeds things up but reduces capacity. These interact with readiness probes: a pod counts as available only when ready, so a good probe prevents traffic going to a broken version and stalls the rollout, which is the desired failure mode. I also set progress deadline seconds and min ready seconds, so that a bad rollout is flagged and pods must remain stable before the rollout continues.
f: Why set maxUnavailable to zero?
What does minReadySeconds do?

q: How do you achieve graceful shutdown so rolling updates drop no requests?
p: Handle SIGTERM, fail readiness first, delay with preStop to allow endpoint propagation, then drain connections within the grace period.
a: When a pod terminates, removal from service endpoints and the SIGTERM signal happen in parallel, so for a short time traffic may still arrive after the application begins shutting down. To avoid dropped requests, I add a preStop hook that sleeps for a few seconds, giving load balancers and kube-proxy time to stop sending new connections. On SIGTERM, the application stops accepting new work, finishes in-flight requests, closes connections and exits, within the termination grace period which I size larger than the longest request plus the preStop delay. Applications should flip readiness to false at the start of shutdown. For long-lived connections like websockets, clients need reconnection logic. I test this by running a load generator during a rollout and checking for errors. Without these steps, every deployment causes a small burst of 502 errors.
f: Why do requests arrive after SIGTERM?
How do you test graceful shutdown?

q: What are Kubernetes Jobs and CronJobs, and what are their failure modes?
p: Jobs run to completion with retries; CronJobs create Jobs on a schedule. Watch concurrency policy, backoff limit, deadlines and missed schedules.
a: A Job runs pods until a specified number complete successfully, retrying failures up to the backoff limit, which suits batch tasks and migrations. A CronJob creates Jobs on a cron schedule. Common failure modes: overlapping runs when a job takes longer than its interval, controlled with the concurrency policy, where forbid skips a run and replace cancels the old one; jobs that retry non-idempotent work and duplicate effects; jobs stuck without an active deadline; missed schedules after controller downtime, governed by the starting deadline; and accumulating completed pods, handled with history limits and ttlSecondsAfterFinished. Time zones also matter, as schedules default to the controller's zone unless specified. I design batch work to be idempotent, log clearly, alert on failed or missing runs using metrics, and set resource requests so jobs do not starve online services.
f: What does concurrencyPolicy control?
How do you clean up finished jobs?

q: How do you use resource requests, limits and QoS classes to protect critical pods?
p: Requests drive scheduling; limits cap usage. QoS class Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort decides eviction order under node pressure.
tip: Equal requests and limits give Guaranteed.
a: The scheduler places pods using their requests, treating them as reserved capacity, while limits are enforced at runtime. Based on these, each pod gets a Quality of Service class. Guaranteed means every container has equal requests and limits for CPU and memory; Burstable means some requests are set but not equal to limits; BestEffort means none are set. Under node memory pressure, the kubelet evicts BestEffort pods first, then Burstable ones exceeding requests, and Guaranteed last, so critical services should have accurate requests and preferably be Guaranteed. Pod priority classes add scheduling preference and preemption. I base values on observed usage, use the vertical pod autoscaler recommendations, and set namespace quotas and limit ranges so teams cannot deploy unbounded pods. Over-requesting wastes money; under-requesting causes noisy-neighbour problems and evictions. I verify the result in a staging cluster before relying on it in production. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: What is the eviction order?
What do LimitRanges do?

q: What is the horizontal pod autoscaler and what can make it behave badly?
p: HPA adjusts replicas based on metrics like CPU or custom metrics; problems include missing requests, slow metrics, flapping and dependency limits.
tip: CPU percent is relative to requests.
a: The horizontal pod autoscaler periodically compares a metric to a target and computes the desired replica count, within minimum and maximum bounds. CPU utilisation is measured relative to the pod's requests, so without realistic requests the target is meaningless. Trouble comes from several places: metrics lag, so scaling reacts late to sudden spikes; flapping when thresholds are too tight, mitigated by stabilisation windows and scaling policies; slow startup times, so new pods are not ready when needed; scaling on CPU for workloads that are bound by queues or latency, where custom or external metrics such as queue length or requests per second are better; and downstream limits, because scaling the web tier may overwhelm a database. I combine HPA with cluster autoscaling for node capacity, set pod disruption budgets, and load test the scaling behaviour.
f: Why do requests matter for CPU-based HPA?
When use custom metrics?

q: How do you deploy a stateful database in containers, and when should you not?
p: Use StatefulSets with persistent volumes, anti-affinity, backups and an operator, but consider managed services for critical data.
a: Containers can run databases, but the operational burden is real. A StatefulSet gives stable network identities, ordered rollout and per-replica persistent volumes. I add anti-affinity or topology spread constraints to separate replicas across nodes and zones, resource guarantees, PodDisruptionBudgets, and careful storage class selection for performance and expansion. Backups, point-in-time recovery, failover, upgrades and monitoring are the hard parts, so I prefer a mature operator that encodes them, rather than hand-written manifests. Even so, for critical production data I often recommend a managed database service, because the provider handles patching, replication and recovery, and the team's time goes into the product. Self-hosting in Kubernetes is reasonable for development environments, specialised needs, portability or when the team has strong database operations skills. The decision should consider recovery objectives, team capacity and cost. I write the reasoning into the runbook so the on-call engineer understands it. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: What does a StatefulSet guarantee?
When would you choose a managed database?

q: What are Linux capabilities and seccomp, and how do you harden a container with them?
p: Capabilities split root privileges into units; seccomp filters system calls. Drop all capabilities, add back only what is needed, and use the runtime default seccomp profile.
cmds:
securityContext:
  capabilities:
    drop: ["ALL"]
  seccompProfile:
    type: RuntimeDefault
a: Traditional root has all privileges; Linux capabilities divide them into distinct units such as binding low ports, changing file ownership or administering the network. Containers get a default subset, but most applications need none, so I drop all and add back only specific ones, for example NET_BIND_SERVICE. Seccomp restricts which system calls the process may make; the runtime default profile blocks dozens of dangerous calls with little compatibility risk, and I enable it with seccompProfile RuntimeDefault, since by default Kubernetes may run unconfined. Together with a read-only root filesystem, no privilege escalation, running as non-root, and AppArmor or SELinux profiles, these controls limit what an attacker can do after exploiting the application. Pod Security Standards, enforced by admission, set baseline and restricted profiles that bundle these settings. For high-risk workloads, sandboxed runtimes add further isolation.
f: Which capability do you add for port 80?
What does the restricted Pod Security Standard require?

q: What are Pod Security Standards and admission controls, and how do you roll them out?
p: Privileged, baseline and restricted profiles enforced per namespace via labels; roll out in audit and warn modes before enforce.
a: Pod Security Standards define three levels: privileged with no restrictions, baseline that blocks known dangerous settings like privileged containers and host namespaces, and restricted, which follows hardening best practice including non-root, dropped capabilities and seccomp. The built-in Pod Security Admission controller enforces them per namespace using labels, with three modes: enforce rejects violating pods, audit records violations and warn tells the user. To roll out safely, I first label namespaces with audit and warn at the target level, review which workloads violate and fix their manifests, then switch to enforce. For finer or custom rules, such as allowed registries or required labels, I add a policy engine like Kyverno or Gatekeeper. System namespaces may need exemptions. Combining admission controls with CI checks gives early feedback and runtime guarantees. I verify the result in a staging cluster before relying on it in production. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: What are the three modes?
When do you need Kyverno or Gatekeeper too?

q: How do you detect and respond to a compromised container in a cluster?
p: Use runtime detection, audit logs and network telemetry; isolate the pod, preserve evidence, rotate credentials and rebuild from a clean image.
a: Detection comes from several sources: runtime security tools such as Falco that alert on suspicious behaviour like unexpected shells, outbound connections or reads of sensitive files; Kubernetes audit logs showing exec calls or role changes; network flow logs revealing unusual destinations; and image or workload anomalies. On suspicion, I isolate the pod, for example by applying a network policy to deny traffic using a quarantine label, rather than deleting it immediately, so memory and filesystem evidence remain. I capture logs, a filesystem snapshot and the pod specification, check which service account and secrets it could access, and rotate those credentials. Then I look for lateral movement and how it got in, such as a vulnerable dependency. Recovery means replacing the workload from a verified clean image, patching the cause and reviewing detections. A rehearsed runbook and least privilege design reduce the blast radius.
f: Why isolate instead of delete?
What does Falco do?

q: How do Kubernetes RBAC and service accounts apply to workloads, and what are common mistakes?
p: Roles grant verbs on resources; bindings attach them to users or service accounts. Avoid cluster-admin, wildcard rules and default service account tokens.
a: RBAC defines Roles, which list allowed verbs on resources within a namespace, and ClusterRoles for cluster-wide or non-namespaced resources, connected to subjects by RoleBindings and ClusterRoleBindings. Pods act through a service account, and a token is mounted by default. Common mistakes are binding cluster-admin to applications or CI for convenience, wildcard verbs and resources, sharing the default service account across workloads, leaving tokens mounted on pods that never call the API, and granting read access to secrets broadly. The remedy is least privilege: one service account per workload, minimal verbs, namespace-scoped roles, automount disabled unless needed, and short-lived bound tokens. I audit with kubectl auth can-i and tools that analyse effective permissions, review role bindings regularly, and use impersonation to test before rollout. A compromised pod with broad RBAC can become a cluster compromise.
f: Why avoid the default service account?
How do you test what an identity can do?

q: How do you scan and control third-party container images in an organisation?
p: Use an approved internal registry, mirror and scan upstream images, enforce signatures and allowlists at admission, and rebuild regularly.
a: Pulling arbitrary images from public registries exposes the organisation to malware, outdated software and rate limits. I establish an approved path: a curated internal registry where upstream images are mirrored after scanning, with a process to request new base images. Scanners check for known vulnerabilities, secrets and misconfigurations on push and continuously afterwards, since new CVEs appear daily against old images. Policies set thresholds, for example blocking critical fixable vulnerabilities, with an exception process that has expiry dates. At admission, a policy engine only allows images from approved registries, requires digests or signatures, and rejects latest. Teams build on a small number of hardened, centrally maintained base images that are rebuilt regularly and distributed automatically. This reduces the attack surface, makes patching systematic, and gives security teams one place to answer which workloads contain a given vulnerable library.
f: Why scan continuously, not only at build?
What does an exception process look like?

q: What is the difference between a Deployment, ReplicaSet and Pod, and how does a rollout use them?
p: A Deployment manages ReplicaSets, which manage Pods; each rollout creates a new ReplicaSet and scales old ones down.
a: A pod is the smallest deployable unit, a group of containers sharing network and storage. A ReplicaSet ensures a specified number of identical pods are running, replacing lost ones. A Deployment adds declarative updates on top: it owns ReplicaSets, one per pod template version. When I change the template, for example the image, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet and gradually scales it up while scaling the old one down according to the rolling update strategy. Old ReplicaSets are retained according to the revision history limit, which makes rollback just a matter of scaling a previous one back up. Because the Deployment controller reconciles these, manual edits to ReplicaSets are overwritten. Changes to labels or selectors need care since the selector is immutable. Understanding this chain explains why deleting a pod just creates another and why rollback is quick.
f: Why does deleting a pod create another?
How does rollback use ReplicaSets?

q: How does the scheduler decide where to place a pod, and how do affinity, taints and tolerations influence it?
p: It filters nodes by constraints then scores the rest; node affinity attracts, taints repel, anti-affinity and spread constraints distribute replicas.
cmds: kubectl describe pod p | grep -A10 Events

tolerations:
- key: dedicated
  operator: Equal
  value: gpu
  effect: NoSchedule
a: Scheduling has two phases. Filtering removes nodes that cannot run the pod: insufficient requested CPU or memory, unmatched node selectors or affinity, untolerated taints, volume zone mismatches or port conflicts. Scoring ranks the remaining nodes using factors like resource balance, image locality and spreading, and the pod goes to the best. Node affinity and selectors attract pods to nodes with certain labels. Taints on nodes repel pods unless they have a matching toleration, which is used to dedicate nodes, such as GPU or system pools. Pod affinity and anti-affinity place pods near or away from others, and topology spread constraints distribute replicas evenly across zones or nodes, which is better for high availability at scale. When a pod stays pending, the FailedScheduling event explains which filters failed, guiding whether to add capacity or relax constraints.
f: What is the difference between a taint and affinity?
How do spread constraints help availability?

q: What are ConfigMaps and Secrets, and what are the security limits of Kubernetes Secrets?
p: Both inject configuration; Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted by default, so enable encryption at rest, restrict RBAC and prefer external secret managers.
cmds: kubectl get secret db -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d
a: ConfigMaps hold non-sensitive configuration and Secrets hold sensitive values; both can be exposed to pods as environment variables or mounted files. Secrets are only base64-encoded in the API, and by default stored unencrypted in etcd, so anyone with read access to the object or etcd can read them. To harden, I enable encryption at rest with a KMS provider, restrict RBAC so few identities can read secrets, limit who can exec into pods, and avoid putting secrets in environment variables when files are an option, since env vars can leak through process listings and crash dumps. A stronger pattern is using an external secret manager with an operator or CSI driver that syncs or mounts secrets at runtime, with rotation and audit logs. Never commit secrets to Git, even in encoded form; use sealed or encrypted formats for GitOps.
f: Why isn't base64 security?
What are the benefits of an external secrets operator?

q: How do namespaces, ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges support multi-tenancy?
p: Namespaces separate teams; quotas cap aggregate resources; limit ranges set defaults and bounds per container.
tip: Namespaces are not a security boundary alone.
a: Namespaces provide a scope for names and a unit for applying policy. Resource quotas cap the total CPU, memory, storage and object counts a namespace can consume, preventing one team from exhausting the cluster. Limit ranges set default requests and limits for containers that omit them and enforce minimum and maximum sizes, so quotas work smoothly. For real multi-tenancy I add RBAC scoped to the namespace, network policies for default-deny traffic, Pod Security admission, separate service accounts and, where tenants are untrusted, node pools or even separate clusters, because namespaces share the kernel, control plane and some resources. Cost allocation uses labels and namespace-level reporting. Governance such as naming conventions, owner labels and automatic provisioning through templates keeps things consistent. The level of isolation chosen depends on trust: internal teams can share a cluster, while external customers often need stronger separation.
f: Why are quotas and limit ranges used together?
When do you need separate clusters?

q: What is a Kubernetes operator or CRD and how is it different from a Helm chart?
p: A CRD adds a new resource type; an operator is a controller that manages it continuously. Helm templates and installs manifests but does not run ongoing logic.
a: A custom resource definition extends the Kubernetes API with a new type, such as a Postgres cluster. An operator is a controller that watches those custom resources and continuously reconciles the real world to match, creating pods, configuring replication, taking backups and handling failover, encoding operational knowledge in software. Helm is a package manager: it renders templates with values into manifests and installs them as a release, with upgrade and rollback, but after install it does not react to changes or failures. They complement each other: it is common to install an operator with Helm, and then manage instances with custom resources. I use Helm for packaging and deploying applications, and operators for complex stateful or lifecycle-heavy systems. Writing an operator is a significant maintenance commitment, so I prefer proven community operators.
f: Can Helm and operators be used together?
What does a reconcile loop do?

q: How do you scan, sign and promote container images in a pipeline?
p: Build once, scan, sign the digest, push to a registry, and promote the same digest across environments, verifying at admission.
a: After building and testing, the pipeline pushes the image tagged with the commit and records its digest. Then it scans for vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, failing on policy violations. If it passes, the pipeline signs the digest, ideally keyless with the pipeline's identity, and attaches an SBOM and provenance. Promotion between environments or registries copies or references the same digest, so what was tested is exactly what runs, and the signature remains valid. In the cluster, an admission policy verifies signatures and optionally attestations, rejecting anything not produced by the official pipeline. I keep production credentials out of build jobs and use separate registries or repositories per stage with different write permissions. Retention policies clean up old images, but images that are currently deployed or needed for rollback are protected. This creates a traceable chain from commit to running container.
f: What does signing prove?
What do you check at admission?

q: How do you run integration tests with containers in CI using Testcontainers or Compose?
p: Start real dependencies in disposable containers, wait for readiness, run tests, and tear down.
tip: Wait for health, not just start.
a: Integration tests are more realistic with real dependencies such as databases and message brokers than with mocks. In CI I start them in containers, either through Docker Compose with health checks and the wait option, or through Testcontainers, a library that starts containers from inside the test code, picks random ports, and cleans up automatically. The important part is waiting until the service is truly ready, using health checks or log-based waits, not just until the container has started, which is a common source of flaky tests. Each test run uses fresh containers and data, so tests do not depend on previous state, and I tear everything down with volumes removed. Pinning image versions to match production avoids surprises. To save time, containers can be shared per test suite with data reset between tests, and I cache images in the CI environment.
f: Why wait for health, not start?
What does Testcontainers add over Compose?

q: How do you do multi-architecture image builds (amd64 and arm64)?
p: Use buildx with QEMU emulation or native builders to produce a manifest list so each platform pulls the right image.
tip: Native builders beat emulation for speed.
a: With ARM nodes becoming cost-effective, images often need to support both amd64 and arm64. Buildx builds for multiple platforms and pushes a manifest list, an index that points to the image for each architecture, so clients automatically pull the right one. Cross-building can use QEMU emulation, which is simple but slow for compilation-heavy builds, or native builders on machines of each architecture combined into one build, which is faster. Cross-compilation inside the Dockerfile, using the target platform arguments, is the fastest for languages like Go and Rust. I make sure every dependency and base image supports both architectures and test the arm64 image, not just build it, since subtle differences exist, for example native libraries or performance characteristics. In the cluster, node selectors or the mixed-architecture manifest ensure scheduling works correctly. I write the reasoning into the runbook so the on-call engineer understands it. That keeps the behaviour predictable for everyone on the team.
f: What is a manifest list?
Why prefer native builders?

q: How do you manage image tagging and retention policies in a registry?
p: Tag immutably with commit SHA and semantic versions, protect release tags, and expire old untagged or unused images.
a: I tag every build with the commit SHA, which is unique and traceable, and add human-friendly tags like semantic versions for releases. Tag immutability prevents anyone from overwriting a tag, so version 1.4.2 always means the same image. Moving tags like latest or environment names are avoided for deployments, and manifests use digests. Retention policies prevent unbounded storage growth: delete untagged images after a few days, keep the last N builds of a branch, expire pull request images quickly, and retain release images for the support period. Lifecycle rules must not delete images currently deployed or needed for rollback, so I align them with the deployment history. Access control separates who can push, typically only the pipeline, from who can pull. Vulnerability scanning and replication to other regions are enabled where needed. Good hygiene lowers cost and makes audits simpler.
f: Why enable tag immutability?
What must retention never delete?

q: How do you deploy the same image to multiple environments with different configuration using Helm or Kustomize?
p: Keep the chart or base generic and supply per-environment values or overlays; promote only the image reference and config changes via Git.
tip: Config differences should be small and visible.
a: The principle is one artifact and several configurations. With Helm, a single chart takes a values file for each environment covering replicas, resources, ingress hosts and feature settings, plus the image reference. With Kustomize, a base holds the common manifests and overlays patch environment-specific fields. These files live in Git, so every difference between environments is reviewed and auditable. Promotion means changing the image digest or chart version in the next environment's values via a pull request or an automated bot, and the deployment tool applies it. I keep the differences minimal and explicit to avoid environment-specific surprises, validate rendered output with a linter and policy checks in CI, and run helm diff or kubectl diff to preview. Secrets come from an external store, not values files. This yields repeatable, reviewable deployments and a clear answer to what is different in production.
f: How do you preview changes before applying?
How do you handle secrets in values?

q: How do you design container logging so logs survive pod restarts and remain searchable?
p: Write to stdout and stderr in structured form; a node agent ships them to a central store with metadata, retention and rotation.
tip: Do not write log files inside containers.
a: The twelve-factor approach is to write logs as an event stream to standard output and error, and let the platform collect them. The container runtime stores them on the node with rotation, and a node-level agent such as Fluent Bit or the Cloud Logging agent tails them, enriches each line with pod, namespace, node and labels, and ships them to a central system like Loki, Elasticsearch or a cloud service. This way logs survive pod restarts and node loss, and developers can search across all replicas. Using structured JSON logs with consistent fields such as level, message, trace identifier and request identifier makes filtering and correlation much easier. I configure rotation limits to avoid filling node disks, set retention and sampling to control cost, and avoid logging secrets and personal data. For apps that insist on writing files, a sidecar can stream those files to stdout.
f: Why log to stdout?
What fields should every log line have?

q: Which container and Kubernetes metrics should you alert on, and which only on dashboards?
p: Alert on symptoms such as errors, latency and saturation risks; keep resource detail like per-container CPU on dashboards.
a: I page on symptoms that affect users or will soon: elevated error rate and latency against SLOs, pods not ready for longer than a threshold, crash looping, persistent volume predicted to fill within hours, node not ready, and failing deployments or jobs. Resource saturation alerts, like memory approaching the limit, are useful as tickets or warnings because they indicate future problems but are not always user-facing. Detailed data, such as per-container CPU, network throughput, restart counts and throttling, belongs on dashboards for investigation, not on pagers. Key metric sources include cAdvisor and kubelet for container resources, kube-state-metrics for object state, node exporter for hosts, and application metrics for RED signals. I tune alerts using burn rates and durations to avoid flapping, and include a runbook link and a dashboard with every alert so the responder has immediate context.
f: Which alerts should page someone?
What does kube-state-metrics provide?

q: How do you use kubectl debug and ephemeral containers to troubleshoot a running pod?
p: Attach a temporary container with debugging tools to an existing pod's namespaces, without restarting or changing the image.
a: Production images are often minimal or distroless with no shell, so I cannot exec into them with useful tools. Ephemeral containers solve this: kubectl debug adds a temporary container to the running pod, sharing its network namespace and, with the target flag, its process namespace, so I can see processes, check network connectivity, inspect files through the process root path and run tools like curl, dig, tcpdump or strace. It does not restart the pod or change the original container. I can also create a copy of a pod with a modified command or image to reproduce a crash, and debug a node by starting a privileged pod with the host filesystem mounted. Access is controlled by RBAC and should be audited, since it grants powerful capabilities. I remove debug artifacts afterwards.
f: What does the target flag do?
Why restrict access to debug?

q: How do you set up readiness, liveness and startup probes correctly to avoid restart storms?
p: Startup probe protects slow starts, readiness controls traffic, liveness restarts only deadlocked processes; do not check dependencies in liveness.
tip: Liveness should be cheap and local.
a: Each probe has a distinct job. The startup probe gives slow-starting applications time to initialise, and until it succeeds, liveness and readiness checks are held off. The readiness probe decides whether the pod receives traffic; failing it removes the pod from service endpoints without restarting it, which is right for temporary overload or dependency problems. The liveness probe restarts the container when it is stuck beyond recovery, such as a deadlock. The classic mistake is making liveness depend on downstream systems like the database: when the database slows down, every pod fails liveness, restarts and the whole service goes down, amplifying the incident. Liveness should check only the process's own health, be cheap, and have generous thresholds and timeouts. Readiness can include critical dependencies. I also tune timeouts to realistic response times under load to avoid false failures.
f: Why shouldn't liveness check the database?
What does a startup probe protect?

q: How do you trace a request across containers and correlate traces with logs and metrics?
p: Propagate trace context headers, instrument with OpenTelemetry, put trace IDs in logs, and use exemplars to link metrics to traces.
tip: Trace ID in every log line.
a: Each request carries a trace context, standardised as the W3C traceparent header, which every service reads and forwards, so spans from different containers join into one trace. I instrument services with OpenTelemetry, using auto-instrumentation where available and manual spans for important operations, and send data to a collector that batches, samples and exports to a backend. To correlate with logs, the logging library adds the current trace and span identifiers to each log line, so I can jump from a slow trace to the exact logs, and vice versa. For metrics, exemplars attach trace identifiers to histogram samples, linking a latency spike to example traces. Sampling is important for cost: head sampling is simple, tail sampling in the collector keeps slow or error traces. Consistent service naming and resource attributes like pod and version make analysis much easier.
f: How do traces and logs get linked?
Why use tail sampling?
